headlines.title: Brush fire spreads to home in the Oakland Hills
headlines.description: A small brush fire spread to one home in the Oakland Hills Tuesday before firefighters were able to stop its forward progress. The Oakland Fire Department (OFD) said the blaze broke out at about 11:45 a.m. along the 1000 block of Panoramic Way, located above the UC Berkeley campus. Forward progress was stopped by about 1:15 p.m. Flames burned through vegetation on a hillside before spreading to the roof and siding of a home along Panoramic Way, according to the fire department. More than 70 firefighters from multiple jurisdictions responded to the scene, ultimately stopping the fire at roughly an acre and a half. “Crews did a fantastic job,” OFD Chief Damon Covington said. “This had potential to take off and be a large-scale event. The multi-jurisdiction response was seamless.” No evacuation orders were issued, but residents on Panoramic Way were asked to temporarily shelter in place. No injuries were reported. The cause of the fire wasn’t immediately known.

headlines.title: ‘We want ICE out': Advocates rally after immigration agents detain man in San Francisco
headlines.description: People packed the steps of San Francisco City Hall Tuesday to denounce what they called a dangerous detention by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on city streets. Security camera footage of Monday’s detention showed three people – one wearing a plaid shirt and holding a gun along with two uniformed and masked ICE officers – approach a man on a sidewalk. One of the agents could be heard asking the man why he was running. The man responded by saying it was because he didn’t know them. The agents then took the man into custody as he repeatedly shouted, “I’m a U.S. citizen.” According to the San Francisco Public Defender’s Office, the man who was detained is their client, but officials wouldn’t share details about why agents may have detained him or if they have made contact with him since he was detained. “We’re still trying to figure out what’s going on in the case,” Deputy Public Defender Francisco Ugarte said. “The issue isn’t this one person. The issue is around the way ICE is making arrests.” During Tuesday’s rally at city hall, Ugarte did not elaborate on questions about a statement ICE released to media outlets about the man who was detained. In that statement, ICE claims the man they arrested, 51-year-old Milton Ramos-Ramirez of El Salvador, has a conviction for voluntary manslaughter in California and may have ties to the Sureños street gang. At the rally, supervisors pledged to quickly pass a supplemental funding measure to go to immigration rapid response teams in the city. “We are here today because it has come to our front door,” Supervisor Jackie Fielder said. “We are here today because in San Francisco, we do not stand for hate. We are here because we want ICE out of San Francisco.”

headlines.title: Motorcyclist dies in solo crash on Highway 85 in Los Gatos
headlines.description: A motorcyclist died in a collision over the weekend in Los Gatos, the California Highway Patrol said Monday. On Saturday just after 3 p.m., CHP officers responded to a collision on the northbound state Route 85 to state Route 17 transition road. According to investigators, a motorcycle driver failed to properly traverse the cloverleaf transition and instead drove off the roadway. The exact time and cause of the crash are currently under investigation, the CHP said.

headlines.title: Sinking roadway raises concerns about another sinkhole in Moraga
headlines.description: The makings of a sinkhole have surfaced in Moraga, where a portion of roadway has begun to sag in an area that has seen sinkholes before. As part of its current storm preparations, the town noticed the sagging roadway while inspecting the area where a previous sinkhole caused major problems. The town of Moraga closed the portion of road Monday, and vehicles can no longer use the entrance to the shopping center. The road is sinking slightly, but town officials are concerned it could give way if vehicles continue driving over it. In March 2016, heavy El Niño rains eroded the soil around a failing 8-foot metal storm drain pipe that ran underground. That caused the road to collapse, bringing down a traffic signal pole and rupturing a PG&E gas line. Another portion of the storm drain pipe failed in 2019, causing another sinkhole. That one was on private property in the parking lot of a gas station, and the owner was responsible for repairing it. The latest occurrence is also on private property, so town officials said the owners of the shopping center are responsible for repairing the pipe underneath the new portion of sinking street. “At this point, I think the concern is the weight of heavy vehicles on that area,” Moraga Police Chief Jon King said. “We are monitoring it as well as the property owner and their engineers. Everybody’s keeping an eye on it. And if it changes, our response would change. As of right now, closing the area to vehicle traffic is what we have deemed necessary.” Stars Gas Station owner Azad Amiri said he believes the roadway will eventually collapse. “This thing is gonna go down because I remember here it happened the same,” Amiri said. “It goes down and eventually it collapse. It’s a big hole.” Moraga’s public works director said repairs on the sagging roadway will begin Wednesday.

headlines.title: Multi-day treasure hunt kicks off in San Francisco
headlines.description: Keep your eyes peeled, San Francisco. A multi-day treasure hunt featuring thousands of dollars in prizes kicked off Tuesday. Rare coin dealer Stack’s Bowers Galleries is hiding prize certificates at iconic locations across the city every day through Saturday. The company will post clues on its Instagram page each day at noon. If you find a certificate, you can redeem it for rare coins or other collectibles, with some prizes valued at up to $3,500.

headlines.title: Palo Alto tightens restrictions on overnight RV parking
headlines.description: Palo Alto is getting stricter with RV parking on public property, with more residential streets set to become off-limits. The city has been working to curtail RV and other large vehicle parking on city streets. New no-overnight-parking signs will go up around Palo Alto’s city limits, announcing parking restrictions on streets within 100 feet of residential areas, including areas zoned for housing and mixed-use sites. There will be no parking between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., doubling the hours when parking is restricted. The city estimates there are about 150 RVs on city streets that people are living in.One issue the City Council will revisit is the 100-foot zone. “It’s not just an arbitrary number, but I think that there’s some considerations there in terms of how you do the actual measurement of that as well and also how it affects each neighborhood,” Councilmember Ed Lauing said. The council will return to the issue in two weeks.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: Motorcyclist dies after crashing into light pole in San Mateo
headlines.description: A man driving a motorcycle died after crashing into a light pole in San Mateo on Monday evening, according to police. The crash was reported at about 5:30 p.m. on Franklin Parkway east of Baze Road. The motorcyclist, a 25-year-old man from San Mateo, succumbed to his injuries and his name has not been released. San Mateo police said a preliminary investigation found that speed was likely a contributing factor in the crash, which happened while the motorcycle was heading east on Franklin Parkway. The road was closed for nearly three hours during the investigation into the crash, police said.

headlines.title: Sen. Adam Schiff raises concerns after SFO immigration holding facility visit
headlines.description: U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff toured an immigration holding facility Tuesday at San Francisco International Airport, where he says some travelers are being held longer than policy allows and without being able to communicate with family or legal counsel within a reasonable timeframe. Schiff says the same thing is happening in Southern California. The senator said the Department of Homeland Security has been using a holding area to detain immigrants for longer than the 72 hours allowed when Customs and Border Protection flags them upon returning from international travel. Schiff says some of those being detained are lawful U.S. residents who get stuck in the system. NBC Bay Area’s Kris Sanchez has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Santa Clara Valley Water declares emergency ahead of potential winter storms
headlines.description: Valley Water declared a precautionary emergency in Santa Clara County to prepare for potentially severe winter storms and flooding. The declaration follows Gov. Gavin Newsom’s statewide emergency proclamation last month, which was prompted by forecasts of a strengthening El Niño pattern that could bring above-average rainfall to Northern California. The emergency allows Valley Water to quickly purchase equipment, stockpile flood supplies and secure services to protect infrastructure. Valley Water since June has been doing stream maintenance and has hit roughly 150 location to prevent possible flooding during the winter months. The agency said the maintenance usually ends in mid-October, but the dry month has allowed crews to continue their work. Residents are encouraged to prepare emergency plans, sign up for alerts and locate free sandbag stations ahead of winter. “Be flood ready,” Valley Water Interim CEO Melanie Richardson said. “Know what you have to do to prepare for an emergency and be ready.” For more information, visit valleywater.org/floodready. headlines.title: SFDA charges construction company, 3 supervisors in deadly 2023 trench collapse
headlines.description: A construction company and three project supervisors were charged in the death of an employee who was crushed when a trench collapsed in San Francisco in 2023, the district attorney’s office said Monday. Alameda County resident Javier Romero, 25, was killed after he became trapped under 8 feet of dirt when a trench collapsed in the area of Oak and Divisadero streets in San Francisco on Sept. 28, 2023. According to prosecutors, Romero was working on a sewer upgrade project in a 2.5-foot wide, 5-foot long, and 8-foot-deep trench that was not properly supported, and when a vehicle drove by, it collapsed. Romero worked for D’Arcy & Harty Construction Inc. and was part of a project for the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission, according to the district attorney’s office. Charged in his death with allegations of involuntary manslaughter and violations of safety standards are San Francisco residents John Darcy, 62, and John Tobin, 39, and Richmond resident Filiberto Poblano Perez, 52. D’Arcy & Harty Construction Inc. was also charged in connection with the death. All three defendants and the company have pleaded not guilty. Darcy was the site safety representative designated by the company and Tobin was the project manager. Poblano Perez was the crew foreman who directly supervised Romero, prosecutors said. According to the district attorney’s office, the state workplace safety inspector who reviewed the fatality concluded that the 8-foot-deep excavation in which Romero died was not properly supported. The short sides of the trench facing Oak Street on one side and facing a building on the other side were completely unsupported, prosecutors allege. The long sides of the excavation running perpendicular to Oak Street were only partially supported. D’Arcy & Harty Inc. had been the subject of a safety complaint about an inadequately supported trench on another project less than three weeks before the excavation collapse that killed Romero, according to prosecutors.
headlines.source: Katy St. Clair | Bay City News

headlines.title: Bonta advises against crypto ATMs, warns of prolific scams
headlines.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta warned residents Monday to be on the lookout for several different types of fraud and scams related to cryptocurrency that have been reported recently. The advisory came as part of an ongoing effort by the Attorney General’s Office to keep the public informed about risks associated with cryptocurrency. Americans lost about $11.4 billion to cryptocurrency-related scams in 2025, according to the FBI’s Internet Crime Center. Bonta’s advisory came days after a settlement was announced between the Attorney General’s Office and Fidelity Digital Asset Services that resolved complaints that the company was restricting customers from withdrawing funds when they wanted to. A similar settlement was reached with Robinhood Crypto in 2024. Bonta declined to say at a press conference in San Francisco’s Potrero Hill neighborhood on Monday whether there were any other investigations into other companies engaged in similar activity. But he warned of a variety of scams and “red flags” that residents in the state should be aware of related to the crypto industry, including those that use artificial intelligence to mimic a familiar person’s appearance or voice, and so-called “meme coins” that are backed – or appear to be backed – by a celebrity or influencer. Such cryptocurrency coins are known for a type of scam called a “rug pull,” in which the issuer of the digital currency attracts investors, driving up the price, before suddenly selling a large share that lets them make a profit but drives the price down for investors, making the coins essentially a way to transfer wealth to the issuer. Recent instances of allegations of rug pull scams have been leveled against President Donald Trump, former president Joe Biden’s son, Hunter Biden, and influencer Hailey Welch, known as the Hawk Tuah Girl. Rug pull scams are also perpetrated by online groups that enthusiastically back a coin and hype it to other online users, only to sell their shares and devastate new investors. Bonta singled out cryptocurrency ATMs as one of the riskiest crypto products and said they should never be used. The machines allow users to buy, sell, and transfer cryptocurrency in-person by accessing digital “wallets” that are used as crypto accounts. They are often placed in businesses by third party companies that Bonta said skirt consumer protection laws because of the anonymous nature of cryptocurrency wallets. There are at least 60 in San Francisco, according to the state Department of Financial Protection and Innovation. Many of them are located in Safeway grocery stores. While operators are supposedly licensed by the state and therefore publicly available, visits to multiple local stores and a Google search revealed there are likely many more than the state’s list shows. In response to a question about legislation to ban the machines, Bonta said it would be up to policy makers to craft such a bill and he would not comment on hypothetical legislation. But he said while they are in operation, crypto ATMs should be universally avoided. “Never use a crypto ATM,” Bonta said. “Never use them. Don’t use crypto ATMs. Scammers push victims to these machines because, once the money goes in, it can’t be reversed, it can’t be easily traced. These ATMs are not backed by trustworthy companies and lack consumer protections.” Vermont, Tennessee, Minnesota, and Indiana have passed legislation banning the machines. In California, the city of San Diego is considering local legislation to require scam warning signs on the ATMs, which are also referred to as kiosks. Bonta said other scams to be aware of include what is known as “pig butchering,” which involves a person pretending to be a love interest who requests large sums of money from victims. “Sextortion” occurs when someone threatens to release compromising material, such as photographs or videos, in exchange for money or some other demand. Bonta advised victims of such scams to ignore threats and block anyone making them. He said the maneuver is most often a bluff, and that the material is rarely released. “Liquidity mining” is a type of scam that promises passive income by connecting a real digital wallet to a fake one, and is often deployed on gaming platforms. The scam involves displaying a fake dashboard to make the user think they are collecting small amounts of cryptocurrency over time, only to see their real assets wiped out. He said other classic scam routines such as gaining a person’s trust through phone calls and other contacts and obtaining passwords or other sensitive information have also been reported, in some instances targeting a previous scam victim by pretending to be someone who can help them recover their money from the first scam. Beware of promises of large returns for small investments, be cautious about unsolicited emails or phone calls and do not provide personal information, Bonta advised. Verify the contact with the source before providing any information by calling the purported business directly and double-checking email addresses. Pause and take nine seconds before acting. The signing of Senate Bill 1208 in early October by Gov. Gavin Newsom will help the Attorney General’s Office have new tools to recover stolen cryptocurrency, according to Bonta, who sponsored the legislation. He said the law would make it easier for investigators to access stolen funds. “It allows them to petition a court to return the cryptocurrency to victims, even when the perpetrators are outside of US jurisdiction,” he said. Bonta also urged victims not to be embarrassed, as scams have proliferated and become sophisticated and have entrapped a variety of victims. Scams involving cryptocurrency and other types of financial manipulation can be reported to the Attorney General’s Office at oag.ca.gov/report.
